title: Enums and Option
summary: Define a type by listing its possible variants, put data inside variants, add methods to enums, and meet Option<T>, Rust's replacement for null.

sections: TRPL 6.1 The Option Enum and Its Advantages Over Null Values
PR ch10 Rich Data Structures Using Enums

blocks.md: A struct says "a value has **all** of these fields". An **enum** (short for *enumeration*) says "a value is **one** of these variants". An IP address is either version 4 or version 6, never both. A shape is a circle or a rectangle. A network message is a ping, a text, or a disconnect. Whenever you would describe something with "either ... or ...", an enum is likely the right type.

blocks.explain: Variants live in the enum's namespace, so you write `IpAddrKind::V4`. Both values have the same type, `IpAddrKind`, which is why one function can take either.

blocks.title: Variants can carry data
blocks.md: An enum's power comes from putting data directly into each variant, and each variant can hold a different kind and amount of data. An IPv4 address is four bytes; an IPv6 address is usually written as text:

blocks.explain: Each variant name works like a function that builds an instance: `IpAddr::V4(127, 0, 0, 1)`. Without enums you would need a struct with a kind field plus fields for both formats, with half of them always unused.

blocks.md: Variants can look like any kind of struct: no data, a tuple, or named fields. Here is one enum for every message a small chat program sends:

blocks.explain: As with structs, enums can have methods in an `impl` block. Four separate structs could hold the same data, but then no single function or array could take "any message".

blocks.title: How big is an enum?
blocks.md: *Programming Rust* explains the memory layout: an enum value stores a small integer **tag** that says which variant it is, plus enough space for the largest variant. `Message` is as big as its largest variant plus the tag. Rust also optimizes common cases: `Option<&T>` is the same size as `&T`, because a reference can never be zero, so zero can mean `None`.

blocks.title: Option: a value that may be missing
blocks.md:
Many languages have **null**, a special value meaning "nothing here". Its inventor, Tony Hoare, called it his "billion-dollar mistake": any variable might secretly be null, and using it as if it were a value crashes the program, often far from where the null came from.

Rust has no null. Instead the standard library defines an enum:

```rust
enum Option<T> {
    None,
    Some(T),
}
```

`<T>` means `Option` works for any type (generics are chapter 10). It is so common that `Some` and `None` can be used without the `Option::` prefix.

blocks.title: Why Option is better than null
blocks.md: An `Option<i32>` is **not** an `i32`. You cannot add it to a number, call number methods on it, or pass it where an `i32` is expected:

blocks.explain: That is the point. Wherever a value might be missing, its type is `Option<T>`, and the compiler makes you handle the `None` case before you get at the `T`. Everywhere else, a plain `T` is guaranteed to be there. The next lesson shows how to handle both cases with `match`.

blocks.title: |v| v * 2
blocks.md: `|v| v * 2` is a **closure**: a small unnamed function, here taking `v` and returning `v * 2`. Chapter 13 covers closures in depth; for now, read `|args| body` as "a function of args".

blocks.title: One type, several shapes
blocks.md: `Shape` has a `Circle` variant. Add a `Rectangle { width: f64, height: f64 }` variant, and in `main` add `Shape::Rectangle { width: 2.0, height: 3.5 }` to the list. The `describe` method already uses `match`, which you will study next lesson; add an arm for the rectangle following the circle's example.
hints: Add the variant with named fields: `Rectangle { width: f64, height: f64 },`.
If you add the variant but not the arm, the compiler tells you `Shape::Rectangle { .. }` is not covered. That check is what makes enums safe to extend.
The arm: `Shape::Rectangle { width, height } => format!("rectangle {width} x {height}"),`.

questions.q: When is an enum a better fit than a struct?
options: When a value has several fields at once
When a value is exactly one of several alternatives
When data lives on the heap
questions.explanation: Struct: all of these. Enum: one of these.

questions.q: Which variant definitions are valid inside an enum?
questions.explanation: Variants can have no data, tuple data or named fields. The last one is not Rust syntax.

questions.q: What is the type of `None` in `let a: Option<String> = None;`?
questions.explanation: `None` is a variant of `Option<String>`; the annotation tells Rust which `T`.

questions.q: You can use an `Option<i32>` directly in arithmetic, like `Some(2) + 3`.
questions.explanation: You must first handle the `None` case and get the `i32` out.

questions.q: Why does Rust use `Option` instead of null?
options: A missing value has a different type, so the compiler forces you to handle it
Null cannot be stored in memory
questions.explanation: Only `Option<T>` can be missing, and you cannot use it as a `T` until you check.

points: An enum is one of several variants: `enum IpAddrKind { V4, V6 }`; write `IpAddrKind::V4`.
Variants can carry data of different shapes: none, tuple-like, or struct-like.
Enums can have methods in `impl` blocks, like structs.
Rust has no null. `Option<T>` is `Some(T)` or `None`, and an `Option<T>` cannot be used as a `T` until you handle `None`.

terms.def: A type whose value is exactly one of a fixed set of variants, each of which may carry data.
One of the alternatives listed in an enum, like Some or None.
The standard enum Some(T) | None, used for values that may be absent instead of null.
An anonymous function written |args| body, which can be passed to methods like map.
